intro: Excerpts copied verbatim from the live source (C:\Users\renne\Downloads\DIGITIZATION COSTS\index.html). Everything runs client-side in one HTML file: pricing lives in a data table, calc() turns inputs into three scenarios, and the result is rendered and exported as a signed PDF report. No server, no database.

snippets.title: RATE_DEFS — every unit rate is data, not code
snippets.explanation: The single source of truth for pricing. Each definition carries a key (k), label (l), unit (u), default value (d), category (c), source citation (s), and an optional assumption flag (a). Because rates are data, Document Imaging & Services can re-price the entire tool from the Configuration tab without touching code, and any value with no published market price is tagged as an assumption.

snippets.title: loadRates — defaults overlaid with saved edits
snippets.explanation: Builds the active rate map R by starting from the built-in defaults and overlaying any values the user saved to localStorage. The guard (key must exist and parse to a finite number) means a corrupt or stale saved file can never inject junk rates — unknown keys and non-numeric values are silently ignored.

snippets.title: gather — read the form into a typed object
snippets.explanation: Collects every input field into one typed object the calculator can consume. Volume is computed as the page-count override when given, otherwise boxes x pages-per-box. Numeric fields are clamped with Math.max so a blank or zero can't break the math, and the eleven hybrid 'who does what' selects are bundled into inp.hy for Scenario B.

snippets.title: Volume and index-unit derivation
snippets.explanation: Turns the raw profile into the quantities the scenarios need. Index units are pages/pages-per-bundle in bundle mode, else pages/avg-pages-per-document. A fringe multiplier wraps all student wages, available weekly student hours (cap) drives the timelines, and condition/depth pick the right per-page rates. Volume >= 100,000 pages flips scanning to the high-volume vendor tier.

snippets.title: Scenario A — vendor full service with a minimum-fee floor
snippets.explanation: Each scenario is an array of line items (label, qty, unit, rate, amount) summed to a total. Scenario A is pure vendor work — scanning, prep, optional OCR, and indexing all priced per page — plus a minimum-fee adjustment if the service subtotal falls below the vendor's floor, then BU's own procurement, PM, and import effort. Its timeline is procurement lead time plus vendor turnaround.

snippets.title: Scenario B — hybrid per-service: vendor rate OR student hours
snippets.explanation: The core of the hybrid model. For each service the user assigned, the code pushes EITHER a vendor line priced as rate x pages, OR a BU-student line priced as hours x wage x fringe (accumulating buHrs). vendorUsed records whether any 3rd-party service was chosen, which later decides whether contract-procurement effort is added.

snippets.title: Scenario B — the structural cost of the two-step path
snippets.explanation: Why hybrid quietly costs more. Because files land outside OnBase, Scenario B always carries two project-management efforts, a DRIP import configuration, and a rework factor (default 15% of student hours) for adapting Phase-1 output to Phase-2 — the hidden overhead of the current two-tier PaperVision practice, made explicit on every estimate.

snippets.title: Scenario C — in-house, single-pass scan + index
snippets.explanation: The scenario the tool is built to favor. Students prep and then scan-and-index in a single pass directly into an OnBase scan queue (siHrs uses the direct scan+index throughput), so there is no share folder, no DRIP import, no second indexing project, and no rework. Its timeline is just queue-setup lead time plus the work divided by available student hours.

snippets.title: Shared in-house labor & hardware sub-calc
snippets.explanation: Converts page volume into student hours via throughput planning factors, shared by Scenarios B and C. Prep and scanning are paced per page; post-scan indexing (Scenario B) is paced per document; the direct scan+index pass (Scenario C) has its own combined throughput. Hardware drops to $0 when the department already owns a compatible scanner.

snippets.title: Pick the cheapest and compute savings
snippets.explanation: Computes savings of in-house versus each alternative and finds the cheapest scenario with a reduce. When Scenario C wins (the common case) it shows a green banner with dollar/percent savings and weeks saved; when it does not, an honest amber banner names whatever is actually cheapest for that volume rather than overstating the in-house case.

snippets.title: Budget check — which scenarios fit, best value first
snippets.explanation: When a budget is entered, the three scenarios are sorted ascending and filtered to those that fit. The lowest-cost fitting scenario is recommended as the best value within budget; if none fit, the closest option and the shortfall are reported with guidance to raise the budget or reduce scope — so the tool never just fails silently.

snippets.title: paginateReport — split into letter-size pages
snippets.explanation: Builds the on-screen 'paper' preview by appending report blocks to a page div until it exceeds ~11 inches, then starting a new page. The keep-with-next loop carries any trailing heading(s) onto the next page so a section title never strands at the bottom. The actual PDF uses the browser's own print pagination.

snippets.title: Storage safety shim — never let a blocked store crash the tool
snippets.explanation: Runs before anything else. It probes localStorage and sessionStorage by writing and removing a test key; if a host blocks storage (sandboxed iframe, private browsing, SharePoint embed) the access throws and the shim swaps in an in-memory store. The tool then works fully for the session and just won't persist between visits in that locked context.
